chapters.label: Before you begin
chapters.title: A Note on the Text
paras: This work is a narrative retelling of the events recorded in the Biblical Book of Judges, specifically chapters 19 through 21. While the overarching historical framework, key figures, and major outcomes adhere to the canonical scriptural account, this book is a work of theological fiction and midrashic expansion.

The dialogue, internal monologues, character motivations, and specific interpersonal dynamics depicted herein are products of the author’s imagination, designed to explore the psychological and spiritual dimensions of the text. This narration does not claim to represent the literal, verbatim words of the divine or the historical figures involved, nor does it assert doctrinal authority over the interpretation of these events.

Readers are encouraged to consult the original Biblical texts for the foundational account. Any resemblance to actual persons, living or dead, beyond those established by scripture, is entirely coincidental.

chapters.label: Chapter 1
chapters.title: The Question of a King
paras: They called him ‘Sar ha-Séder, Melekh ha-Tóhu,’ the Prince of Order, the King of Chaos. And though his titles seemed to cancel one another, in him they were entwined, bound together as fire and smoke. Where others saw contradiction, he saw design. It was known that he was born not to dwell within the balance of things but to remake the times by his equilibrium.

From childhood, there was something in his gaze that unsettled everyone. His was not the stare of a child, wide with wonder, but the predatory analysis of a hunter, analyzing, baiting, and waiting. While others played with swords and fought make-believe enemies, he arranged his pebbles in patterns; his reeds, line upon line, as though his mind were naturally inclined to rehearse the very architecture of war.
He had a way of listening to silence, of dissecting nothingness, until all things cowered before him. The neighbors said he was cursed. His parents found him peculiar.

He learned early what it took years for most to learn: that men are ruled by virtue, debased by desire, restrained by fear and unconstrained by love. And he had chosen, with this knowledge, who he wanted to be.

He barely laughed or cried. Did not bother about showing what he felt because he did not care. There was strategy in all his actions, and all he did was toward an utterly devised end. He was unlike his kin and belonged to a different arithmetic, one where what could be was constantly weighed against the necessity of what was, and necessity always won.

He did not walk in the false liberty of the times. To him, the disorder was an invitation. The void of law and the silence of God were a table set, and he had a ferocious appetite, leashed, for dread he might devour himself if fed. For his will to tyranny was equal to the zeal of his pure conscience.

He grew into manhood as though worshipped by the gods of time. His voice deepened, his shoulders broadened, and beyond that, his thoughts scintillated into arrows that could pierce the wisdom of the wisest men of the times.

He spoke less than most, but his words were as prophecies impossible to ignore. Some loved him for it. Others hated him. But all men feared him. And while most bleed when cut, he did not. He burned with a raging determinism that devoured until his vengeance was settled in blood and smoke.

Those who knew him before history changed his name said, during those last days, he changed, shrouded by the aura of forbidden deaths and bloodcurdling horrors he'd reserved for those who'd caused him pain. He walked, and time stopped, like he hauled a thousand demons with each step. He grew quieter and ceased to pray, ascending from petty rage and vengeance to a colder, divine plane beyond good and evil. And when the desert winds blew, it was said that he was waging war with the lovers of some heathen god.

Years later, when the war was over and generations who did not know him were born, they would view the annals of history, and seeing the deaths of 25,000 men and the near annihilation of a tribe of the sons of Jacob, would ask: Who is he to have wrought such a fearsome thing?
And those who recalled bits of the story passed down from father to son would say, 'Mélekh ha-Métim,’ King of the Dead.
The story goes that Israel in those days had no king, and every man did what was right in his own eyes.

Most squirmed as the orange turned into a bright yellow that burned the dust until it clung to their throats like it did their clothes. The tent of meeting stood afar off, an uninterested witness in today's affairs, its linen stretched taut, reluctantly swallowing and spitting out whoever came or went.
Each tribe had sent men to represent them. Their cloaks were woven with colors that told their lineage's heritage.
Saar ben Mattithiah walked with dignified silence among the others, his pure white apparel gliding effortlessly past the others as if in discriminatory prejudice, fearful to contaminate itself.
He was not powerful like the rest. Not a trader or a warrior. He was the simplest of men and, at those times, one of the few who were looked upon by some with disdain. A priest.
When he was close to the entrance, Saar turned to the boy beside him and placed a hand on his shoulder. “Wait here. These matters are for the council alone.”
The boy nodded once and left.
At the tent’s threshold, Saar stilled, and his eyes closed briefly. When he opened them and entered the room, his gaze was gentle and illuminating, like that of a lamp in a darkened room.

The boy remained in the sun, his eyes tracing the assembly of children in the courtyard. Most of them, like him, had accompanied their parents here. Some of the younger ones played, chasing one another, tossing fruit, laughing with joyful voices. Their world was still simple, unaffected by the politics of hunger or greed.
He stood apart, his arms folded in reflexive silence. His gaze drifted to the hills beyond the horizon, where the land shimmered in the heat.

He had been there when his father heard the news. Rumors of fields failing, families starving, whole villages turning hollow-eyed with famine. An unnatural hunger caused by human hands. That was why the council had gathered.

The tribe of Ephraim had pleaded to the rest of Israel for help. Their land was a harsh, rocky hill country where the soil was thirsty, where a man’s harvest could vanish with a single season of drought.

When crops failed in the previous year, there had been little to fall back on. Ephraim was landlocked with no coast to trade by sea and no wide valleys for momentary yields. Their survival depended on the roads, lifelines that carried supplies between the tribes, and when there were no rains, they turned their efforts to mining and trade. But those roads ran through Benjamin, and for some years now, Benjamin had altered its trade policies, only allowing those to pass who had something to give. And so they pleaded, because an act against Benjamin was one against Abner ben Kelah, and everyone sought to gain his favor. So Ephraim’s cry had become Israel's problem.
But why was Israel as it was?

The older generation said that things had been better during the time of Joshua. Now they said there was disorder because there was no king. But that was the story they told themselves. Wasn’t Yahweh their King already? Had He not led them by fire and cloud? Torn down walls, sent bread from heaven, and separated the sea itself? What king could match such miraculous wonders that they sought such a man to rule?
He frowned as his thoughts deepened. Maybe the answer wasn’t that profound. It had to be simple. The people forgot. They'd forgotten because they had become blind to God's providences.

His mother often told him that he was special because he had in him the virtues of the men of Issachar, who were gifted to understand the times. He wondered if that was why these patterns appeared clearly to him.
His eyes returned to the other children again as they laughed and shouted, their games vivid with life. For a moment, he almost envied them.

Inside the tent, muffled voices rose. The men were deliberating, more like arguing. He hoped his father’s voice could share some wisdom, a piece of truth that could help the tribes. Father often said that peace was hard to keep and war easier to start, but peace was precious and had to be kept by all means. Levi agreed but was tempted not to fully believe.

If there is no king in Israel and that disconcerted the people, then God will raise one. Maybe not a king in the political sense, whom the people will love, but one who will do what must be done, just as the other judges had always done.
His eyes were gazing at his feet when a commotion interrupted his thoughts.

Just beyond the courtyard, a boy a bit younger than him was cornered by a group of older boys. He looked to be from Ephraim. They were obvious to spot these days with their patched tunics and thin faces.

The older boys laughed as they shoved him to the ground. One snatched at his small leather pouch, tearing it from his belt. The boy cried out, clutching for it, but a kick to the ribs sent him curling in the dust. Coins spilled, a meager handful, and were snatched up by greedy fingers.
“Seems dogs eat better than you Ephraimites these days,” one jeered.
He observed them a while, then turned away to leave. Trouble was nothing he sought.
“There!” one of the boys shouted, pointing at him. “Another one trying to scram.”

They turned as one, eyes glinting with cruelty. These Benjamites seemed to have more training in arrogance than etiquette. They walked toward him with the foolish swagger of those who placed trust in the outcomes of an uncertain world.
“Well… what do we have here?" one sneered. “A humble Levite.”
“A priest-boy.” Another scorned.
“What do you people still pray about?” One asked, “Nobody's listening.”
The boys kept speaking as they circled him. Their words vexed him, not because he believed them, but because they bore the popular sentiments of the times. The people had stopped believing in God.
He stood still, his arms at his sides, his lips twitching.
“You speak much,” he began, “but say nothing. Perhaps you are still too young or just too ignorant to—”

A blow from a boy in the group landed on his face and stopped his words. Their laughter faltered for a moment as the leader of the group stepped forward. He was taller, about a year older than he was, with aristocratic cheekbones and arrogant eyes. His black curls framed a face too proud for childhood.
He was the Prince of Benjamin, Malchi ben Abner, son of Abner ben Kelah.
Malchi studied the boy in front of him with narrowed eyes while his companions waited for his word.

“I’m sure you think yourself clever,” Malchi began. “But clever words will not change what you are nor the times you're in, Levite. You who preach only of law and wait for others to sow so you can inherit one-tenth of all our spoil. You think yourselves our equals, we who feed you?”
His jaw tightened, but he would not give them the pleasure of his anger.

“You do not feed me. You have not fed us for a generation. Nor were we ever yours to feed. The Lord of hosts, Yahweh, whose name is mighty, is He who feeds us and delights us in His abundance. But you will know little of God's abundance, you who steal from others to have what to eat and think yourself wiser for it.”

The boys muttered. Malchi’s face had darkened. He stepped closer until he stood inches from the boy. For a moment, they faced off in a terrible silence, and then Malchi’s hand struck across his face in a deliberately stinging insult.
He staggered, and blood sprang from his lip. The laughter of the others returned, cruel and triumphant.

His fists clenched. His heart beat like a drum in his chest. A thousand thoughts raced through him, with one growing louder: strike him down. But even as the fire rose, another thought restrained him: to fight him is to fight all of Benjamin. He steadied himself. He would not give them a victim.

At that moment, the council tent opened, and Saar ben Mattithiah stepped out, his face still weary with the stress of debate. He looked upon the situation, and his shoulders sagged; a faint tremor lingered in his hands when he lowered them from his robe. Fine lines marked the corners of his eyes, deepened by the strain, and his breath came slow and heavy. His eyes stayed a while on his son's face, then moved to the jeering circle of Benjamite boys, Malchi standing smug at the center.
Saar’s jaw tightened, and then he approached, his head inclined with dignity, an unusual presence among the restless boys.

“Peace, sons of Benjamin,” he said, his hand lingering tightly at the fold of his robe. “Forgive my son. I hope he has not caused you undue hurt with his words. I hope we will not make enmity out of it.” He bowed to Malchi. “Let us forgive what has passed.”
The boys smirked, and Malchi sneered, then hissed. Slowly, with laughter still on their lips, they drifted back toward the courtyard, coins jingling in their hands.
“Why, Father?”

His chest tightened, heat rising under his skin until each breath was sharp and shallow. His fists curled at his sides, nails pressing into his palms, his jaw locked, teeth grinding against one another, his eyes fixed unblinkingly on Malchi. A flush crept up his neck, his entire frame straining as his body begged him to retaliate, while his feet held their ground.
“Why?” Levi asked again.
“Walk with me.”
Saar placed a gentle hand on his son's shoulder.
“You know why,” he said when they were at a distance.

“That boy is Malchi ben Abner, whose father currently commands the entire tribe of Benjamin. His vineyards feed the land. His warriors guard the roads. His silver pays the judges. To quarrel with his son is to quarrel with all of Benjamin and perhaps half of Israel. Peace, son. Peace at all costs.”
Peace… that was all his father cared about. It was useless trying to talk him into considering matters from another perspective.
“The council, what was decided?” He asked.
Saar’s shoulders sagged. “Nothing has changed. Benjamin is unyielding, and none dare raise a hand. Unless the LORD Himself moves to intervene, we are bound constantly at Benjamin’s mercy.”
At their mercy. So this was going to be it for the rest of this generation too?
They walked on in silence, father and son, the dust rising at their feet.

Only the weak are asked to keep the peace, always told to bow down and wait. The strong mock the law, and the elders soothe them with apologies. Perhaps respect and understanding are only the language of the oppressed. The powerful speak only in threats and violence.

His young heart wrestled with the thought. He wanted to believe his father was right, that patience, prayer, and hope would deliver Israel. He wanted to believe that the LORD would act and all would be well, but—
Saar squeezed his son’s shoulder. “In time, it will happen. Just you wait. The LORD sees everything.”

chapters.label: Chapter 2
chapters.title: An Unloved Son
paras: Malchi pulled aside the tent’s flap and hesitated a while before entering. Inside, the air was warm and carried the scent of baking bread mingled with the faint musk of sheep's wool. His mother sat cross-legged near the hearth, her fingers busy with a spindle of flax. Beside her were his twin sisters, Naamah and Tirzah, five years younger than him, their faces lit by the glow of the small fire. Their voices had been a stream of chatter with high notes of laughter, but when Malchi stepped inside, they fell silent.

His mother’s hands stilled, the spindle slowing. Naamah’s lips parted, but Tirzah’s hand brushed hers quickly. They observed him briefly, then turned back to their tasks as though nothing had happened.

Malchi stood for a while, then turned to go. At the entrance, he paused, the leather flap in his grip. He could hear the faint rasp of the spindle resuming its movement and the whispered scrape of the twins sorting dried dates into a jar. His chest rose once, shallow, and then again, slower. The sound of his breath slipped out, rougher than he had meant it to be. The flap sagged from his hand, whispering shut against the tent’s frame as he sauntered out.

The sunlight struck his eyes, harsher than before. The boys who had been with him loitered in a circle near the cooking pits, tossing stones. He sighed and started moving towards them. In truth, he despised them, but they were tolerable.
Their laughter grew when they noticed him. He gave them a small smile. He had learned long ago that most people laughed too easily and at nothing of importance.
He was about to follow them toward the far end of the encampment when a voice cut through the air.
“Malchi.”
His back stiffened, breath locked high in his chest. His neck turned with a slow grind, shoulders rigid, eyes sliding toward the sound with a hard blink.
His father, Abner ben Kelah, strode from the direction of the council. His frame filled the path, his golden linen cloak snapping in the breeze with each step.

Men shifted aside at his approach, their eyes lowered, hands pressed briefly to their chests. Women drew their children closer to get them out of his path. He moved through them without pausing, not wasting a glance. His beard, trimmed and streaked faintly with grey, framed a mouth pressed flat, lips thinned to a line that gave no room for warmth.
“What have you been doing?” His voice was clipped at the edges. His nostrils flared as he spoke.

Malchi’s throat closed, a dry click rising as he tried to swallow. His tongue stuck against the roof of his mouth, lips parting without a sound before he forced out a word. “Nothing,” he muttered, his voice breaking.
The word had scarcely left his lips when Abner’s hand landed on his cheek with a crack. Many turned and stopped what they were doing to watch.
Malchi’s head jerked to the side, his cheek flushing red. His knees bent under the blow, legs trembling before he forced himself upright, eyes locked on the dust at his feet.
The surrounding boys froze. A woman pulled her child close and hurried past. No one spoke. The space around them widened, the silence holding all movement still.
“You disgrace me,” Abner said. “Is this what I have labored for? For you to be the one who takes all I've worked for and turns it to waste?”
Malchi clenched his fists but did not lift his eyes.

Abner’s voice cut deeper, escaping through his teeth. “If your brother still lived, if you had not killed him, he would have been better suited to inherit it all. He had a sense of responsibility that you will never learn.” His spit hit the dust, and his hand flexed open and shut at his side, shoulders rigid. “You are shame itself. A stain on my house.”

Malchi’s head lowered further. His fingers dug into his palms until the knuckles blanched, the muscle in his jaw twitching. Around them, the boys did not move, their eyes darting from father to son, unwilling to meet either gaze.
“I am sorry, Father,” Malchi whispered. Malchi whispered. The words were hollow, bones without flesh.

“Sorry?” Abner laughed scornfully. His eyes narrowed. “You say sorry while you loiter about like a fool?” His hand struck his chest. “Look at you! If you had a mind worth sharpening, you would have been in the council, listening, learning. But no—” His breath came hard through flared nostrils as he hissed. “You shame me even upon the very ground where you stand.”
His hand shot out as he pointed to their tent. “Back inside. Go sit where I can see you.”
With that, Abner turned, his stride long and angry, the flap of the tent snapping shut behind him.

Malchi stood, motionless, chest lifting and falling in short, uneven pulls. His shoulders hunched and arms stiff at his sides. The boys kept still, eyes sliding over him, then dropping away. They turned away one by one, breaking the circle, their steps quick as they scattered.
A hand settled on his shoulder, steady. Malchi’s frame tensed beneath it. His breath caught high in his chest before he let it out in a slow release.
“Do not take his words to heart.”

It was Ezra, Abner’s steward. His eyes stayed fixed on Malchi. His mouth did not shift, neither frown nor smile, only a calm set of lips that gave no room for doubt. His hand remained on Malchi’s shoulder, the weight lighter than his father’s words, steadying the boy’s trembling frame.

“I know,” Ezra said, the words pressed close for Malchi’s ears alone. “Your brother’s death was no crime of intent. It was an accident, though your father’s heart will not admit it. Do not let his grief become your guilt.”
Malchi’s lips quivered, his teeth biting his trembling lower lip before he forced himself still. “It is fine,” he said. “I understand.”
Ezra’s hand pressed lightly. “You need not carry this burden alone. In time, he will see. You will grow into a fine young man, terribly fearsome and powerful.”

Malchi looked up briefly. The tent loomed before him, shadows flickering against the linen walls where the fire inside cast its restless glow. From within came the faint laughter of his sisters, and his father’s voice softened now, playful, a tone Malchi scarcely heard turned upon him. He swallowed.
Ezra’s eyes held his, unwavering. “Trust yourself. All will be well.”
The words were kind, but Malchi didn't believe them. But he nodded anyway.

Inside the tent, Abner sat close to the fire, his cloak folded neatly to one side, his back straight, legs drawn firm beneath him. His hand reached toward Naamah and Tirzah, fingers catching their braids, tugging just enough to pull laughter out of them.

Naamah bent forward, covering her mouth with both hands, her shoulders shaking as she tried to hold her giggles. Tirzah leaned in against him, answering his funny riddles in quick bursts, her voice running high and fast.

Malchi stood at the entrance, half within, half without. His shadow stretched into the tent, but no one beckoned him closer. He watched as Naamah crawled into their father’s lap, clutching a wooden doll, while Tirzah recited a fragment of a psalm she had learned that morning. Their mother, Shua, watched too, her hands resting still upon her knees, her eyes bright with pride. Every so often, she leaned in, brushing back a strand of hair from Tirzah’s cheek, or laughing softly at Naamah’s wild attempt at a song.
The family sat close around the fire, knees nearly touching, their voices overlapping. Malchi remained outside its light.

Ezra entered beside him and gave a small nod, guiding him with a firm hand toward a mat laid in the corner. Malchi lowered himself without protest. He sat with his knees drawn up, his arms folded across them, the fire warming his face, though his chest felt cold. His eyes strayed to the way his father’s hand rested easily on Tirzah’s shoulder, how his gaze lingered with affection on Naamah’s childish smile. A pulse rose in his throat, the muscles pulling hard as he swallowed. His eyes dropped, and he turned his face aside.
Ezra sat beside him, lowering his voice. “Your father returned with a few victories from today's council meeting,” Ezra said.
Malchi nodded, though his ears were not upon Ezra’s words.

Ezra leaned nearer, his tone soft, as though drawing Malchi into a different world. “The famine grows in Ephraim. Their fields continue to fail, and Benjamin’s roads remain closed. It was pleaded that your father yield some measure of grain, but he stands firm. His storehouses must serve his own, he says. And the council fears to push harder.”
Malchi’s eyebrows drew low over his eyes, the skin creasing hard between them.

Ezra continued, unbothered. “The merchants have grown restless. The tribe of Dan will not carry their caravans without heavier tolls, and Judah looks to strengthen their spears. All of Israel is changing, Malchi, because of your father’s power. These councils are not the idle talk you imagine. They are the balance upon which our future rests, and your father’s concern is that you are unable to secure the future he’s creating.”
Malchi’s eyes flickered to him for a heartbeat, then away. He could not help but notice how his father’s hand stroked Naamah’s hair with care and how Tirzah leaned against his shoulder without fear.

Ezra saw it. His voice grew gentler. “I know your heart is elsewhere. But you must learn, Malchi. What your father commands now, one day you will command. These matters will pass into your hands, whether you want them to or not. Best to train your ear while the burden is still his.”
Malchi forced himself upright, tilting his head as though in concentration. “Let us proceed,” he said, though his voice betrayed him.

Ezra touched his shoulder again. “Do not let envy rob you of learning. There is much your father withholds from you, but much still that you may gather. Watch him. Listen. You may think he despises you, but you will see, there is a reason for all things.”
A reason to call me a disgrace? Malchi thought.
“You must endure,” Ezra said, as if reading his mind. “All will be well. Believe me.”
The fire dimmed as the night darkened, the shadows stretching long across the tent walls. Ezra leaned closer. “Listen. These are matters you cannot afford to ignore.”
“I'm listening,” Malchi sighed.

“The roads,” Ezra went on to the fourth lesson, his hands folded calmly on his knees, “are the heart of Benjamin’s strength. Your father controls them: every caravan, every cart, every sack of grain that passes from valley to hill.”
Malchi swallowed. He knew these things in fragments but hadn't given much thought to the role his father played in the larger scheme of things.

Ezra continued, "While your father has much, power such as his is brittle. Ephraim grows desperate, and desperation breeds recklessness. Already, men speak of rebellion. Should they rise, Judah will not stay silent. And if Judah rises…” He let the thought hang.
Malchi’s brow furrowed. “War. The men of Judah are men of war.”
Ezra nodded. “War. And a war within Israel is a war that will not favor anyone.”
From the hearth, Naamah stirred in her sleep, murmuring something. Abner shushed her gently. Malchi forced his eyes back to Ezra.

“What does that mean for us? There seems to be nothing to do, because if we appease, we give way, and that makes room for more leeway. But if we also do nothing, the outcome might still be unfavorable."

“We can increase our sway within the council,” Ezra said. “Your father has sent gifts to some houses. They will urge the people to wait longer. In the meantime, we will cause discord in Ephraim to turn them away to problems other than their desperation.”
Malchi’s jaw clenched. He wanted to speak and then decided to hold his tongue.

Ezra studied him, his voice softening. “You are so much like your father, and that is a good thing. He's hard on you as he is on everyone else. He believes softness is rot, and he would rather you bear scars than be unfruitful.”
Malchi’s throat burned. “He does not see me at all. He sees only what my brother left.”
Ezra placed his hand once more on Malchi’s shoulder. “You are his heir, whether he scorns you or not. One day, he'll acknowledge you.”
Malchi raised his head slightly, eyes searching Ezra’s calm face. There was no deceit in the man's gaze as he proceeded.

“Politics, Malchi, is not only speeches and councils. It is bread, water, and land. These are the stones upon which nations are founded. One day, you will stand where your father stands, and men will look to you, some for bread, others for judgment. You must learn what you can now to know what to do then. The future is always uncertain.”
“That was your first lesson,” Malchi said.
“I'm glad you're now paying attention.”

chapters.label: Chapter 3
chapters.title: Thorns and Thistles
paras: The hill country of Ephraim gave little to those who tilled it. The ground was stony, the soil shallow. Crops failed often, and the barns were near empty. In the villages, children’s arms thinned, voices lost their vibrance, and men spent more time speculating over hope than working because there was nothing left to tend. Women leaned over clay jars and scraped the bottom for what little grain remained, and food was sold at prices that drove the just to melancholy and the unjust to crime.

To leave one’s home was bitter, but to stay was death. Eliab, past his youthful prime but not yet overtaken by age, sat in his house and counted what coins he had left. His wife, Dinah, watched from the side, her hands still atop her lap, her lips pressed tightly. Their daughter Miriam, 12, sat on a stool near the door, her chin tucked to her knees. The air between them carried no sound except the faint scrape of Eliab’s thumb rubbing over the coins.
At last he spoke, “We cannot remain here. Tomorrow we leave for somewhere else, where, perhaps, we will find food and work.”
Dinah’s fingers curled into her garment. She looked at Miriam, then back to her husband. “And if there is nothing there for us?”
Eliab’s teeth clenched. “Then we go somewhere else. But we will not die.” His eyes flicked to the empty jars lined along the wall.
Miriam had been silent. Now she raised her head, her eyes wide, fixed on her father. “Will there be food there at least?” Her voice was thin and cracked.
Eliab reached across and touched her hair. “Yes, my girl,” he said. “Food enough to make you into a plum.”

They left at dawn. Two bundles held their clothes and what little they still owned. Eliab carried the heavier one, Dinah the smaller. Miriam walked between them, with a small bundle, her eyes shifting from side to side, scanning every turn in the road, her grip tightening on her mother’s hand as they traveled inland.
By midday, the straps had rubbed Miriam's skin raw. She tried not to complain, but her limp gave her away. Her mother bent often to check her feet, urging her along with words of comfort.

The first day, they found a caravan on the road. The merchants allowed the family to walk within their company until evening. Eliab spent two of his last coins on a round of flatbread and dates. They ate in silence, breaking small pieces for Miriam first. Her mother chewed slowly, her face set, as if holding herself back from hungering for more.
That night they lay by the roadside with Miriam pressed close to her mother, and her father curled around them, one arm across both.

The second and third days passed slowly. Miriam’s pace slowed more, and Eliab carried her often, shifting her weight across his shoulders. When she walked again, she dragged her feet, her eyes glassy from heat and weariness. Her mother's face was drawn, the hollows under her cheekbones sharper. She rubbed her hand across Miriam’s back whenever the girl stumbled, even though her own steps faltered.

By the fourth day, their food was gone, but the road bent toward Ramathaim. The walls and roofs of the Levite town came into view as the sun sank, the last light stretching thin across the ground. Miriam leaned against her father’s side, her head bumping against his arm as she walked, half-asleep.
They entered the city at nightfall. Lamps burned behind shutters, and the streets were scanty.

Eliab pleased with strangers, one after another. “Do you know where we may find a place to rest?” The words pressed out urgently. One man shook his head and walked on. Another waved them away. A woman pulled her child close and did not even answer. Eliab asked five in all, but none offered help. By the fifth, his eyes dimmed, and he ceased asking.

They wandered to the edge of the street where a tree leaned beside an abandoned house. Its roof sagged, and weeds grew along its walls. Eliab dropped his bundle against the base of the tree. His hands trembled as he spread his cloak on the ground. “Here,” he said softly. “We will sleep here tonight.” His voice cracked at the end.
Dinah lowered herself with Miriam in her arms. The girl shivered and asked, "Will it be better here, Mama?”
Her mother swallowed, her chest rising unevenly. “Yes, Miriam. Better days will come.” She glanced at her husband, her eyes damp.
Eliab crouched beside them. He cupped Miriam’s cheek with rough hands. “Do not be afraid, my girl,” he said. “Tomorrow we will feast. We will find work and all will be well.”

The sun bore down on the hills as Saar ben Mattithiah stood, bent at the waist, his hands pressing soil around young barley shoots on one of his three fields. His tunic clung to his back with sweat, his eyes moving carefully over each row, pressing the soil with patient hands. The small nod he gave at the sight of the plants showed his satisfaction.

He straightened from the furrows, brushing soil from his palms, and lifted his eyes toward the slopes beyond the farms. Levi was there, moving with the herd. The boy’s shouts carried faintly down the hill, hoarse from yelling. Saar watched a moment longer, then, satisfied that the fields were tended to and the flock was safe under his son’s care, he left the farm and started home.
It was already past sundown when Levi brought the herd down and guided them into the pen. After latching the gate, he bent down to the trough, splashed his face with water, and went into the house.

He paused at the doorway, his brows drawing together, his hand resting against the frame before he leaned in slightly, his head tilting as he listened, curiosity pulling him forward. Strangers rarely entered their house, and it usually wasn't for anything good. He cleared his throat and walked in.

At the table were the unfamiliar faces of a man and a woman. Their garments were frayed, and their faces bore the dull look of hunger and exhaustion. The man’s beard was unkempt and streaked with grey. His shoulders sagged forward, his arms resting heavily on his knees. The woman’s eyes were hollow and her lips were cracked, but she sat upright.
Levi’s mother, Hannah, poured them water, her movements joyful as always.
“Shalom,” Levi greeted, his eyes flicking to his father’s for an explanation.
Saar lifted his head from the cup in his hands. “These are travelers from Ephraim,” he said. “They don't have a place to stay.”
Levi nodded and turned to the man, his posture reserved.
The man inclined his head. “I am Eliab. This is my wife, Dinah. We thank you for your hospitality.”
Levi's mother sat near them, eager to start a conversation. “You will eat and rest here tonight. Whatever burden you carry, leave it for tomorrow.”
Eliab’s shoulders eased slightly, but his eyes still darted to the floor. Dinah pressed her hands together and murmured her thanks again.
Levi lowered himself onto a bench, still quiet. His eyes flicked to their bundles stacked by the wall, then his breath caught as he looked up.

The scent of soap and freshwater from within reached him before the footsteps. A girl emerged from inside, her damp hair falling over her shoulders, her cheeks flushed. She stepped into the doorway and paused when she noticed Levi.

In that pause, Levi stiffened, and the world fell silent. His lips parted slightly, but no words came. The girl did not drop her gaze. Her eyes, bright and unguarded, fixed on his with a curiosity that made his face burn. His fingers twitched, and he shifted slightly on the seat.
It was his father who broke the silence with a chuckle. “This is spectacular! My son, abashed by a girl. Perhaps there is hope for my lineage after all.”
The others laughed lightly.

Levi came to and dropped his eyes to the table, his jaw clenched. The girl’s cheeks turned rosy, and she moved quickly toward the only available space, beside Levi. Her hand brushed against his as she sat. He kept his eyes lowered.

His father kept smiling as he watched them. His mother hid a faint smile behind her hand as her eyes softened at Levi. Dinah glanced between her daughter and the boy, her lips pressing together in thought. Eliab sat straighter, his countenance unreadable.
Levi finally found his voice, though it was low and halting. “Welcome,” he said to her, his eyes still lowered.
“Thank you,” she answered, her voice a breeze over a vast meadow.

The meal finished fast. Everyone was hungry. But no one had yet risen. The table still held scraps, a half-empty bowl of lentils, and the bones of the lamb. The fire burned low, throwing soft light against the walls. For the visitors, the warmth of good food after such a long time was a sense of safety.
Saar broke the silence. “Pray tell, what’s happening in Ephraim these days?”

Eliab inhaled and let it out slowly. “It’s as bad as the rumors say. The land gives little because the rains are scarce. We have endured poor harvests before, but this time it is worse. It's like every other famine, except that the Benjamites now control the roads. They demand tolls that most can't pay. And if you refuse, raiders strip you of everything. Most people who dare the roads are beaten; others do not return at all. And there is no recourse, for Abner ben Kelah commands everything. No one dares resist him.”
Dinah lowered her eyes as her husband spoke. Miriam sat beside her, listening with a stillness uncommon in a child.

Eliab’s voice grew quieter. “We are not Ephraimites. Our roots are in Bethlehem of Judah. But we cannot return there. Our kin are gone, and we have no lands. Ephraim was meant to be our hope for a new start. But… so, seeing how it was, we decided to sojourn elsewhere for another chance.”

Saar stroked his beard, his eyes fixed on Eliab. “The actions of Benjamin press upon many. You are not alone in this suffering.” He paused, then added firmly, “But you will not sleep in the streets again. Tonight, you will rest under my roof, and tomorrow I will speak with some of the town's men. There is always work in Ramathaim for men looking for honest labor."
Eliab bowed his head. His chest rising and falling with sharp breaths. “You do more than I can ask of you. My thanks will never be enough.”

Levi's mother turned to Miriam. Her voice was soft. “Child, you will not be idle either. I keep a small apothecary. If you are willing, you may come with me, and I will teach you how to prepare oils, how to make perfumes, and how to trade them. It is honest work, and the market sells well.”
Miriam’s eyes brightened. “Yes,” she said quickly. “I will be there. I want to learn.”
Her mother's hand rested briefly on her arm, a trace of pride showing through her tired eyes.
“I will come too,” Dinah added. “If you will have me.”
“You are also welcome,” Hannah said.
The room eased into softer tones as the tension unwinded. Miriam turned to Levi, who sat quietly, his hands in his lap. “And what do you do?”
“Sheep and cattle.” He looked down. “I tend the sheep and goats and keep the herd.” His ears reddened as he spoke.
Saar chuckled, shaking his head. “He spends more time with those animals than with people. I feared he would never look past their woolly heads.”
Levi turned his face away as Miriam’s lips curved into a small smile.
Hannah touched her husband’s arm, her tone carrying a playful rebuke. “Do not jest at him; he just hasn't had time to make friends is all. And you know where His real talents lie.”

Saar laughed lightly. “I jest,” he said. “Our son tends the herds and our farms. It's actually because of his suggestions that our crops and cattle do better each year. He's truly special, a blessing from God.”
Levi's gaze remained fixed on the table to avoid meeting anyone’s eyes, but he risked a glance at Miriam and saw that she was still watching him, her eyes filled with interest.
The conversation flowed on. Eliab shared the details of their journey. Dinah added little, but her eyes shone wet when she spoke, her voice breaking occasionally.
Eventually, the room quieted, and Hannah rose to clear the table, the sound of pottery against wood breaking the silence.

Later, Levi and his mother spread mats across the floor for their guests. Eliab and Dinah lay close, their hands clasped. Miriam curled beside them, her breath shallow, her eyelids heavy but not yet closing.

Levi went to his room to sleep. He turned onto his back, staring into the dim rafters. The voices of the house had faded, but his mind did not. Each time he closed his eyes, Miriam’s face returned and his chest stirred with something restless. His hands pressed against his chest trying to steady it.

He turned onto his side, facing the wall, but sleep would not come. Hours passed as he listened to the faint rustle of his father shifting in their room. When at last his eyes grew heavy, the final image that lingered on his mind was hers. To him, she was the most striking thing he had ever seen, something unique in its beauty that had unsettled his small silent world.
